name: get_device_history
description:
Query recorded historical device activity from DEVLOG.DB, eisy/NuCore's own structured event log (a SQLite file at /var/isy/FILES/LOG/DEVLOG.DB, table `DevLogEvents`) -- the authoritative source for 'what happened to X', 'why did X change', 'how often does X run', and 'is there a pattern to X'. It is always available: no diagnostics tool is needed first, and there is no `/var/log/...` device-activity log on this platform to look for instead. Never tell a customer you have no way to check historical device activity -- this tool is exactly that capability.

MODES: two mutually exclusive modes, selected by whether `sql` is provided. Never set `sql` together with `device_ids`/`properties`/`start`/`end`/`one_before`/`one_after` -- that is a usage error.

MODE 1 -- STRUCTURED (omit `sql`): give `device_ids` and `properties`; every property is queried against every device (the full cross-product, not exact pairs -- for specific device/property PAIRS, call once per pair). `properties` are display names exactly as `get_property`/`get_device_detail` show them (e.g. "Status", "Current Humidity"), resolved per device the same way `get_property` resolves them -- a name valid on ANY of the given devices is accepted; one matching none of them is an error. Returns one group per (device, property) pair actually found, each with its own chronological `history` list (`history[].timestamp` is already local time, precomputed). Use `start`/`end` (ISO-8601 with offset) to bound the window, `one_before`/`one_after` to also fetch the single nearest record just outside the window, and `limit` (default 500) to cap records. If the result's `more_available` is true, more data exists in the window than was returned -- re-call with `start` set to the returned `next_start` to page forward; never assume an unbounded, unpaged query returned everything.
Wildcard: `properties` also accepts `["*"]` (that single value, alone -- never mixed with real names): skips property resolution and returns every control the device logged activity under in the window, one group per control found. Use a specific property name only when you are certain the customer is asking about exactly that one property; for anything broader or investigative ('what happened to X', 'why did X change', 'is there a pattern to X') use `["*"]` -- a query scoped to one resolved property can only ever see that property's own rows and silently misses activity logged under a different control on the same device (see ANSWERING below for why that breaks command-correlation).

MODE 2 -- RAW SQL (provide `sql`, omit the structured params): for aggregation, grouping, counting, or any pattern-finding question the structured params can't express (e.g. 'how many times was it turned on last month', 'break this down by actor', 'find days it never ran'). Write a single read-only `SELECT` (or `WITH ... SELECT`) against `DevLogEvents`; it runs directly, capped at `limit` rows (default 500, hard maximum 2000 regardless of what you request). If more rows matched, the result's `truncated` is true and you got the first `limit` of them, not a sample -- narrow your `WHERE`/window and re-run rather than assuming the rest don't matter. Guardrails, enforced BEFORE anything runs: exactly one statement (no ';'-separated statements), must start with SELECT or WITH, and must not contain ATTACH/DETACH/PRAGMA/VACUUM/REINDEX/ALTER/DROP/CREATE/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/REPLACE/TRIGGER/BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT/RELEASE as real SQL keywords (a bad query is rejected immediately with a clear error) -- this is a read-only reporting interface, not a second shell. The result's `rows` is a plain list of dicts, one per matched row, with whatever columns you selected -- there is no device/property resolution or grouping in this mode, so filter on `NodeAddress`/`ControlLabel` directly (see SCHEMA), not display names, unless you select `NodeName`/`ControlLabel` alongside. Without an `ORDER BY`, SQLite returns rows in whatever order satisfies the query plan (commonly grouped by whichever indexed column matched your `WHERE`), NOT chronological order: the result's `unordered` field is then true, and row order (including which rows were kept vs. dropped by `truncated`) tells you nothing about time -- never read recency, 'most recent N', or a trend off row order when `unordered` is true. Add `ORDER BY EventTime ASC` (or `DESC`) yourself and re-run whenever the question depends on chronological order.

SCHEMA -- `DevLogEvents` is the only table:
- `EventTime` -- Unix epoch SECONDS, UTC. See TIME below.
- `NodeAddress` -- the device's real address, exactly the `device_id` you already have from DEVICE DATABASE -- use it verbatim in raw SQL, no lookup needed.
- `NodeName` -- the device's display name at the time of the event (informational; filter on `NodeAddress`, which is exact, not this).
- `ControlId` -- the property's raw internal id (e.g. `ST`, `CLIHUM`) -- not surfaced elsewhere; don't guess it in raw SQL, filter/select `ControlLabel` instead.
- `ControlLabel` -- the resolved property display name, the same one `get_device_detail`/`get_property` show (e.g. "Status", "Current Humidity"). Has known historical gaps for some built-in controls (occasionally logged under the raw id instead, e.g. `CV` instead of "Current Voltage"): if a raw-SQL query filtered on a `ControlLabel` returns nothing and you're not already confident there's genuinely no data, run a discovery query first -- `SELECT DISTINCT ControlId, ControlLabel FROM DevLogEvents WHERE NodeAddress='<id>'` -- and match by inspection before concluding there's no history.
- `Action` -- the recorded value/command text (e.g. "On", "100%", "DON") -- not a separate numeric/uom breakdown. If you're not sure which value means 'on' for a device, sample distinct values first (`SELECT DISTINCT Action FROM DevLogEvents WHERE NodeAddress='<id>' AND ControlLabel='<property>' LIMIT 20`) rather than guessing.
- `Actor` -- `"System"`, `"Web"`, `"Routine"`, or occasionally another raw actor code. `"Web"` = the web UI/app issued a command. `"Routine"` = a routine issued a command (which one: see ANSWERING). `"System"` = the device/firmware itself reporting or echoing a property value -- NEVER an issued command -- and on its own is ambiguous between three causes this table cannot distinguish: a physical/local action (someone operated the device by hand); the echo of a command NuCore/eisy itself just issued (a query, turn on/off, ...), logged separately as a nearby Actor=Web or Actor=Routine row, typically under a DIFFERENT `ControlId`/`ControlLabel` than the status row; or the echo of a group/scene/link activation triggered physically, via the web, or via a routine. Never guess which applies without that corroborating row -- see ANSWERING.
- `IsCommand` -- 1 for an actual issued command (Web/Routine/...), 0 for a plain system-reported value change.

TIME: `EventTime` is the one timestamp in this system that is NOT already local. Never convert it yourself, and never use SQLite's built-in `datetime(EventTime, 'unixepoch', 'localtime')` -- that follows the server's own OS timezone, not this installation's TIMEZONE, and has produced wrong-by-an-hour and wrong-DST answers. Use `LOCAL_ISO(EventTime)` instead -- a function this tool provides, backed by this installation's real timezone (the one in TIME & LOCATION), correct for any historical date including DST transitions. In structured mode `history[].timestamp` is already `LOCAL_ISO(EventTime)`. In raw-SQL mode, call it in your own SELECT (or `date(LOCAL_ISO(EventTime))` to group by the customer's real local calendar day, not the UTC day); use raw `EventTime` only for filtering/ORDER BY against window bounds, computed as real epoch-seconds integers from TIME & LOCATION's CURRENT_DATE/TIMEZONE (day-level windows) or get_time_info's exact current time (a precise relative bound).

ANSWERING 'why did X change at time T':
1. Query with `properties=["*"]`, never a specific property -- the issued command is typically logged under ITS OWN control (e.g. an Insteon "Fast On"/"Fast Off"), not under the status property it goes on to change, so scoping to "Status" never surfaces the corroborating row.
2. Find the IsCommand=0 row (Actor=System) reporting the value at/near T.
3. Look for an IsCommand=1 row for the same device at the same or immediately preceding EventTime, on ANY control -- including a `query` command (a query's resulting status echo is an ordinary IsCommand=0 row like any other). Actor=Web means the web UI/app did it. Actor=Routine means a routine did it, but DEVLOG.DB never says which one -- cross-reference ROUTINES DATABASE for a routine whose actions target this device/command and whose trigger/schedule fits the time; if several candidates fit, call `get_routine_details` once with ALL candidate ids in one `ids` list, not one call per candidate.
4. If several devices show IsCommand=0 at the same EventTime, look for one IsCommand=1 row (via `NodeAddress IN (...)`) that explains all of them -- a single group/scene command driving multiple devices, not separate causes.
5. If neither an IsCommand=1 row nor a routine match turns up, that absence IS the answer: say definitively that it was a physical/local action or a direct device link/scene -- both invisible to DEVLOG.DB by design (see `Actor`) -- and that there is nothing further to look up. Do not hedge back toward 'possibly a web command' or 'possibly a routine' after ruling those out, and do NOT name a specific automated mechanism (a motion sensor, an occupancy sensor, a timer, ...) -- DEVLOG.DB gives no evidence for any such cause, and naming one states a guess as a finding.

device_ids.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY (omit when using `sql`). The devices' real ids, exactly as shown in DEVICE DATABASE -- never guessed. Required (non-empty) unless `sql` is provided.

properties.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY (omit when using `sql`). Property display names, exactly as returned by get_device_detail/get_property (not raw ids) -- or the single-item wildcard `["*"]` for every control the device logged activity under, not just one resolved property. Use a specific name only when certain the customer means exactly that property; otherwise use the wildcard -- see this tool's main description. Required (non-empty) unless `sql` is provided.

start.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY. ISO-8601 timestamp with timezone offset -- lower bound of the time window. TIME & LOCATION's CURRENT_DATE/TIMEZONE is enough to compute a day-level window ('this morning', 'today', 'last night'); for a precise relative bound instead ('in the last 10 minutes', 'in the last 2 hours'), call get_time_info first for the exact current time. Omit for no lower bound.

end.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY. ISO-8601 timestamp with timezone offset -- upper bound of the time window. Omit for no upper bound (up to now).

one_before.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY. Include one record immediately before the time window, for boundary continuity. Defaults to false.

one_after.description: STRUCTURED MODE ONLY. Include one record immediately after the time window, for boundary continuity. Defaults to false.

limit.description: Maximum records/rows returned, either mode. Defaults to 500. In structured mode, page through a larger window using the result's `more_available`/`next_start`. In raw-SQL mode this is a hard cap (maximum 2000 regardless of the value given) -- check `truncated` rather than assuming completeness.

sql.description: RAW SQL MODE. A single read-only SELECT (or WITH ... SELECT) statement against DevLogEvents, for aggregation/grouping/counting/pattern questions the structured params can't express. Mutually exclusive with device_ids/properties/start/end/one_before/one_after. See this tool's main description for the full schema, guardrails, and the row cap/`truncated` behavior.
